unit.title: Weld using gas tungsten metal arc welding process GTAW - (Tungsten inert gas -TIG)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A WPS for a stainless steel pipe says 'back purge with argon until the oxygen is below the stated limit'. How does the team leader confirm this?
options: By smelling the gas coming out of the vent hole
With an oxygen analyser at the purge outlet
By running the purge for one minute per metre of pipe
By feeling the gas flow on the back of the hand

questions.stem: Why is GTAW often chosen for the root run of a high-pressure steel pipe, even when the fill and cap are done by MMAW?
options: It is the fastest way to fill a thick-walled pipe joint to the top
It needs no shielding gas when used on a pipe root
It lets the welder use any filler rod that is to hand
It gives a clean, fully fused, controlled root with no slag

questions.stem: A job card asks for GTAW on thin copper pipe fittings. Which current and gas are usual?
options: DCEN with argon, or argon-helium for more heat
AC with carbon dioxide, to give a strong cleaning action on copper
DCEP with an argon and oxygen mixture
AC with pure helium and no argon at all

questions.stem: Why do many shops replace thoriated tungsten with lanthanated or ceriated tungsten where the job allows?
options: They are the only types that will work on AC current
They never need to be ground or sharpened before use
They work well and avoid radioactive grinding dust
They allow welding without any shielding gas

questions.stem: High-frequency (HF) arc starting can upset nearby electronic equipment. What should the team leader do before setting up a TIG station beside a computer-controlled machine?
options: Follow the maker's earthing advice and keep TIG leads short and apart
Run the TIG leads alongside the machine's control cables to save space
Switch the HF start on at its highest setting so the arc starts quickly
Remove the earth connection from the TIG set to stop the noise

questions.stem: A pipe joint in a trench is being back purged with argon. What extra hazard must be controlled?
options: Argon burns easily, so no sparks are allowed nearby
Argon makes the pipe too cold to weld in a trench
Argon smells strongly and will make the welder feel ill quickly
Argon is heavier than air and can collect in the trench

questions.stem: A tungsten must be changed during a job. What is the safe order?
options: Change it at once while the arc is still running
Turn the output off, let the tungsten cool, then change it
Pull it out with bare fingers to feel whether it has cooled down yet
Knock it out with a hammer while the machine is on

questions.stem: On an AC TIG machine, what does the balance control change?
options: The gas flow rate through the cup and through the gas lens screens
The share of each cycle spent cleaning or penetrating
The length of the post-flow after the arc stops
The voltage the machine gives with no arc running

questions.stem: What usually happens if the AC balance is set with too much electrode-positive time on aluminium?
options: The pool gets narrow and very deep, with no cleaning
The arc goes out at once and will not restart
The filler rod stops melting into the weld pool
The tungsten overheats and the bead is wide and shallow

questions.stem: On an inverter TIG set, what does raising the AC frequency (for example from 80 Hz to 150 Hz) usually do?
options: Narrows and focuses the arc, which helps on fillets
Widens the arc so it spreads over a larger area
Cuts the amount of argon the torch uses each minute
Makes the tungsten melt into a large ball faster

questions.stem: What does pulsed DC TIG help a welder do on thin stainless steel sheet?
options: Weld without any filler rod or shielding gas at all
Use a much larger tungsten than the job would need
Control the heat and pool, with less distortion
Clean the oxide off the surface during welding

questions.stem: Why is a water-cooled torch used for long TIG runs at high current, such as over 200 A?
options: Water cooling gives a cleaner gas flow over the weld
An air-cooled torch would overheat at that current
Water cooling lets the tungsten be made much thinner
Water cooling stops all the ultraviolet light

questions.stem: What is a gas lens in a TIG torch?
options: A dark glass that protects the welder's eyes
A clear cover that keeps spatter off the cup
A lens that magnifies the weld pool so the welder can see it better
A fine mesh that smooths the gas flow from the cup

questions.stem: When a tungsten for DC welding is ground with a blunter (larger) included angle at the point, what does it usually give?
options: A narrower arc, deeper penetration and longer tungsten life
A wider arc, shallower penetration and a much shorter tungsten life
No change to the arc, only to how the tungsten looks
An arc that wanders badly and is hard to start

questions.stem: Why is a tiny flat ground on the very tip of a pointed tungsten used at higher currents?
options: So that it fits more tightly and evenly in the collet
So the arc starts without high frequency
So the fine point does not melt off into the weld
So the tungsten can be used on both ends

questions.stem: Which tungsten diameter is usually chosen for DC TIG on 3 mm steel at about 100 A?
options: 1.0 mm
2.4 mm
4.8 mm
6.4 mm

questions.stem: Why is helium sometimes added to argon for TIG welding thick aluminium or copper?
options: It is much cheaper than pure argon
It makes the arc far easier to start
It cuts the ultraviolet light from the arc
It gives a hotter arc and deeper penetration

questions.stem: What is a trailing shield used for in TIG welding?
options: To keep gas over the hot weld behind the torch on reactive metals
To hold the filler rod at the right angle to the weld pool
To shade the welder's hand from the light of the arc
To catch spatter before it lands on the finished surface

questions.stem: A stainless pipe joint is to be back purged. Why are both ends of the pipe dammed or plugged, with a small vent?
options: To stop the pipe moving while it is welded
To hold argon in and let air escape as it is pushed out
To keep the pipe warm all through, so that it welds more easily
So the oxygen meter can be fitted inside the pipe

questions.stem: Why is the gap of a stainless pipe joint taped over during purging, with the tape peeled back as the root is welded?
options: So that the gap does not close up from the heat while welding goes on
To mark where the welder should start and stop
To stop argon escaping and air getting in through the gap
So the root can be welded without any filler rod

questions.stem: A procedure says to purge with five times the volume of the purged section. The section holds 4 litres and the flow is 10 L/min. How long should the purge run before welding?
options: About 20 minutes
About 40 seconds
About 10 minutes
About 2 minutes

questions.stem: Which colour on a stainless steel TIG weld usually shows the gas cover was good?
options: Silver to light straw
Dark blue all over
Grey and flaky
Black with a crust

questions.stem: Why is heat input kept low when TIG welding austenitic stainless steel such as grade 304?
options: Stainless steel melts at a much lower temperature than mild steel
A low heat lets the welder use mild steel filler rod
To limit distortion and loss of corrosion resistance
Because the argon will not shield a hot stainless pool

questions.stem: After TIG welding stainless steel, which cleaning restores its corrosion resistance on the heat tint?
options: Grinding with a disc that was used on mild steel
Pickling or electro-cleaning to the maker's instructions
Painting the weld area with a silver-coloured paint
Wire brushing with a carbon steel brush until the metal is bright

questions.stem: Why is thick aluminium (for example 12 mm) often warmed a little before TIG welding?
options: To melt off the oxide skin before the arc starts
To make the tungsten ball up more quickly and give a wider arc
So that the AC balance can be set to zero
It draws heat away so fast that the pool is slow to form

questions.stem: Black specks and a dirty pool appear when TIG welding aluminium. What is the likely cause?
options: Oxide or dirt left on, or too little cleaning action
The current is too high for the tungsten size
The argon flow is set at the normal rate
The filler rod is held too close to the pool

questions.stem: What is 'walking the cup' in TIG pipe welding?
options: Moving the torch away from the pipe between tacks
Changing to a larger cup for each run of the weld
Rocking the cup on the joint edges to move along
Holding the cup still while the rod does the work

questions.stem: When TIG welding an open-root joint, what is the 'keyhole'?
options: The hole drilled at the end of a crack before repair
A small hole at the front of the pool showing full penetration
The vent hole left in the purge dam for the gas
The opening in the end of the cup that the tungsten passes through

questions.stem: Why is a copper backing bar often clamped under a TIG butt joint in thin sheet?
options: Copper draws heat away and supports the root without fusing
Copper adds extra filler metal to the root, so less rod is needed
Copper makes the arc much easier to start on thin sheet
Copper shields the back of the weld from the gas flow

questions.stem: The end of the filler rod has gone dark and oxidised. Why is it cut off before welding starts again?
options: A dark rod will not melt at the usual current
A shorter rod is easier to hold steady by hand
A dark rod would make the tungsten go blunt
The oxidised tip would carry oxide into the weld

questions.stem: When TIG welding a vertical-up fillet, how is the torch usually angled?
options: Pointing down the joint at about 45°
Pointing up the joint, about 10–20° from square
Flat along the joint, almost touching the plate
Square to the plate, with the rod fed from below

questions.stem: What is the main benefit of a foot pedal or torch-mounted current control when welding round a fixed pipe?
options: It lets the welder use a larger tungsten on the pipe
It means no post-flow is needed at the end of a run
The welder can change the heat as the position changes
It stops the arc from wandering on the curved pipe

questions.stem: A TIG weld on carbon steel shows a crack running down the middle of the bead. Which is a likely cause?
options: Too little filler, giving a thin, hollow bead
Too much argon flowing through the cup
A tungsten that was ground too sharp
Too slow a post-flow at the end of the run

questions.stem: A TIG root on carbon steel pipe has excess penetration: a large bead hanging inside the pipe. Which is a likely cause?
options: Too little current for the size of root gap
Too small a root gap with a fast travel speed
Too much argon flowing from the cup
Too much heat or too wide a gap at the root

questions.stem: Lack of penetration is found in a TIG root on a 5 mm wall pipe. Which change would most help?
options: Less current and a faster travel speed
A wider gap or more current, as the WPS allows
A smaller cup and a lower gas flow
Adding more filler rod at the top of the pool

questions.stem: A TIG weld on aluminium shows porosity. Which is the most likely cause?
options: The AC frequency is set too high for the job
The tungsten is pointed instead of rounded
Hydrogen from moisture or oil on the metal or rod
The welder is using a gas lens on the torch

questions.stem: Which method would you choose to find fine surface cracks in an aluminium TIG weld?
options: Dye penetrant testing
Magnetic particle testing
A hardness test
A spark test

questions.stem: A food-grade stainless pipe weld is checked inside with a borescope (a small camera on a lead). What is the inspector looking for?
options: The welder's ID stamp on the inside wall
The colour and width of the outside cap, compared with the drawing
How much filler rod was used on the weld
Full root penetration, a smooth profile and no sugaring

questions.stem: Why is a TIG-welded pressure pipe often given a hydrostatic (water pressure) test after NDT?
options: To clean the inside of the pipe after welding
To cool the weld quickly so that it ends up harder and stronger
To prove the pipe holds its test pressure and to show up any leak
To remove the heat tint from the inside of the pipe

questions.stem: Why is stainless steel stored on wooden or plastic racks, away from carbon steel?
options: Stainless steel bends if it is laid on steel racks
Carbon steel racks make stainless steel magnetic
Iron particles from carbon steel cause rust spots
Stainless steel slides off steel racks too easily

questions.stem: An argon cylinder lasts 10 hours of arc time at a flow of 10 L/min. About how many litres of gas does it hold?
A trainee's tungsten keeps getting dirty because it dips into the pool. As team leader, what is the best coaching?
options: Tell the trainee to use a much longer arc length so the tip stays clear
Give the trainee a bigger cup and more gas flow
Tell the trainee to turn the current right down
Show a braced hand, a steady arc and rod fed without moving the torch

questions.stem: The WPS lists ceriated tungsten, but the store only has thoriated. What should you do?
options: Check whether the WPS allows a substitute; if not, get the right type
Use the thoriated tungsten, since all tungsten types weld the same way
Grind the thoriated one to a finer point so it acts like ceriated
Weld without a tungsten until the right type comes in

questions.stem: Apart from the welder and the settings, what extra record is normally kept for a back-purged stainless pipe weld?
options: The colour of the welder's gloves and jacket
The time of day the cylinder was delivered
The purge gas, its flow and the oxygen reading
The name of the person who swept the bay

questions.stem: At the end of a TIG job, why are tungstens and filler rod offcuts put away labelled by type?
options: So they can be sold for scrap at the best price
So the wrong type is not used on the next job
So the store can count how many were wasted
So they stay warm until the next job starts

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters HF stand for, in TIG arc starting?
What is the name of the argon flow sent inside a pipe to protect the back of the root while it is welded?
What is the name of the thin, tough skin on aluminium that must be cleaned off or broken up before welding?
An oxygen meter on a purge vent reads in ppm. What do the letters ppm stand for?
A TIG root is welded at 90 mm per minute. How many minutes will it take to weld round a pipe whose circumference is 270 mm?
What is the name for the band of colours (straw, blue, grey) left on stainless steel beside a weld?
What is the term for the length of tungsten that sticks out past the end of the cup?
Heat input is often worked out as volts × amps × 60 ÷ (travel speed × 1 000). The answer is given in kilojoules per what?
What is the name of the plug, often made of soluble paper, put inside a pipe each side of the joint to hold the purge gas near the weld?
What do the letters RT stand for in weld testing?
A WPS allows 80–110 A for the root run. The welder has set 125 A. By how many amps is that above the limit?
Name the light, strong metal, used in aircraft and chemical plants, that needs a trailing shield and full gas cover when TIG welded.
In a filler rod code such as ER70S-2, what do the letters ER stand for?
What is the name of a TIG weld where the edges are melted together with no filler rod added?
What is the name of the document that comes with a batch of filler rod or plate, giving its chemistry and test results?

essays.stem: Explain why a stainless steel pipe root needs a back purge, how the purge is set up and checked, and what happens to the root if the purge fails.
essays.modelAnswer: When stainless steel is hot, the air on the inside of the pipe attacks the back of the root. Without a purge the root oxidises into a grey, crusty layer called sugaring, which is weak, rough and loses its resistance to corrosion, so the joint must be cut out. To set up a purge, the pipe ends are cleaned and lined up, and purge dams are fitted inside each side of the joint. The gap is taped. Argon is fed into the space through a hose at the flow the WPS gives, and let out through a small vent so air is pushed out. The purge runs long enough to change the gas several times, and an oxygen meter at the vent must show the level the WPS allows before welding starts. The tape is peeled back as the root is welded, and the purge is kept on for at least the next run. If the purge fails, the root turns dark and crusty and fails inspection.
markingPoints: Explains that air oxidises the hot back of the root (sugaring) and lowers corrosion resistance
Purge dams, taped gap, argon in and a small vent out
Purges for long enough and checks oxygen with a meter before welding
Keeps the purge on during the root and the next run; peels tape as it goes
Describes a failed purge: dark, crusty root that must be cut out

essays.stem: Explain how AC balance, AC frequency and current affect a TIG weld on aluminium, and how you would set them for 4 mm aluminium plate.
essays.modelAnswer: Current sets the overall heat. Aluminium carries heat away fast, so it needs a fairly high current to start a pool, and a foot pedal helps to reduce it as the plate heats up. AC balance sets how much of each cycle is electrode-positive, which breaks up the oxide (cleaning), and how much is electrode-negative, which gives penetration and keeps the tungsten cool. More cleaning gives a wider, frosted band but heats the tungsten; less cleaning gives deeper penetration but may leave oxide. AC frequency controls the arc shape: a higher frequency gives a narrower, more focused arc, useful for fillets and corners, and a lower one gives a wider, softer arc. For 4 mm plate I would start from the WPS or the maker's chart, test on scrap of the same plate, and adjust the balance just enough to give a clean pool, with a frequency that keeps the arc on the joint.
markingPoints: Current sets the heat; aluminium needs enough heat, controlled with a pedal
Balance: electrode-positive cleans the oxide; electrode-negative gives penetration
Effects of too much or too little cleaning
Higher frequency gives a narrower, focused arc; lower gives a wider arc
Starts from the WPS or chart and tests on scrap before welding the job

essays.stem: Compare the main types of tungsten electrode and explain how you would choose and prepare one for AC aluminium and for DC stainless steel.
essays.modelAnswer: Pure tungsten forms a clean ball on AC and was used for aluminium on older machines, but it does not carry high current well. Thoriated tungsten starts well and lasts on DC, but it is slightly radioactive, so its grinding dust must be controlled. Ceriated tungsten starts easily at low current and is good for thin work. Lanthanated tungsten works well on both AC and DC and is a good all-round choice on modern inverters. Zirconiated tungsten holds a ball well on AC. For AC aluminium on an inverter, I would use a lanthanated tungsten of the size the WPS gives, with a slightly blunted point or small ball. For DC stainless I would use lanthanated or ceriated, ground on a grinder kept for tungsten, with the marks running along the length and a small flat on the tip. The type is checked by its colour band and the WPS.
markingPoints: Describes pure, thoriated, ceriated, lanthanated and zirconiated in plain terms
Notes the grinding dust hazard of thoriated tungsten
AC aluminium: suitable type and a blunt or balled end
DC stainless: pointed, ground lengthwise on a dedicated grinder, small flat on tip
Checks the type by colour band and the WPS

essays.stem: Explain why heat input must be controlled when TIG welding austenitic stainless steel, and describe how you would control it and finish the weld for a food-grade job.
essays.modelAnswer: Austenitic stainless steel spreads heat slowly and expands a lot, so too much heat makes it warp. Too much heat, or holding it hot for too long, can also form chromium carbides near the weld, which lowers its resistance to corrosion, and it leaves dark heat tint. To control heat I would use the lowest current that gives full fusion, pulsed current if the machine has it, a steady travel speed, small runs, and copper backing or chill bars. I would tack closely and weld in a balanced order, letting the job cool between runs and checking the interpass temperature. A back purge protects the inside. For a food-grade job the weld must be smooth, with no cracks or pits where dirt can hide. I would blend the weld with stainless-only abrasives and remove the heat tint by pickling or electro-cleaning, as the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules allow.
markingPoints: Explains distortion and loss of corrosion resistance from too much heat
Low current, pulse, steady travel, small runs, chill bars
Close tacking, balanced sequence, cooling and interpass checks
Back purge to protect the inside
Smooth, crevice-free finish; heat tint removed by an approved method

essays.stem: Describe how you change the torch angle, filler feeding and current as you TIG weld a fixed pipe (5G) from the bottom to the top.
essays.modelAnswer: On a fixed pipe I weld each half from the bottom, just past 6 o'clock, up to the top at 12 o'clock. At the bottom I am welding overhead: the torch points up into the joint with a small push angle, the pool is kept small and the current is lower so the metal does not sag inside the pipe. The rod is fed into the front of the pool, and on an open root it may be fed close to the gap to support the inside. As I move up the side (vertical), the torch angle changes to keep pointing up the joint, and I can increase the current a little, keeping the keyhole even. Near the top the pipe is hotter and the position is flat, so I reduce the heat with the pedal and add rod steadily to avoid burn-through. I move my body to stay comfortable, and tie in carefully where the two halves meet.
markingPoints: Welds each half from the bottom to the top
Overhead part: small pool, lower current, torch pushed up into the joint
Changes the torch angle to follow the pipe as it goes up the side
Reduces heat near the top as the pipe gets hotter
Feeds rod at the front of the pool and ties in the two halves

essays.stem: Explain how pulsed TIG works and when you would use it. Describe the settings you would think about and why.
essays.modelAnswer: In pulsed TIG the current switches between a high peak current and a low background current many times a second, or slowly on some machines. The peak melts a spot of metal and the background lets it cool and freeze a little while keeping the arc alive. This gives good fusion with less total heat. I would use it on thin sheet, stainless steel and out-of-position welds, and where distortion or burn-through is a problem. The settings are the peak current, which sets fusion and penetration; the background current, often a fraction of the peak, which sets how much the pool cools; the pulse rate, which sets how often the peak comes (slow pulses make a ripple pattern that helps a welder add rod in time, fast pulses give a stiffer, narrower arc); and the time spent at the peak. I would start from the maker's guide and test on scrap.
markingPoints: Current switches between peak and background
Peak melts; background lets the pool cool while the arc stays lit
Used on thin sheet, stainless, out of position, to control heat and distortion
Explains peak, background, pulse rate and peak time
Starts from the maker's guide and tests on scrap

essays.stem: Describe four defects found in TIG pipe roots. For each, give the cause, how it is found and how it is prevented.
essays.modelAnswer: Lack of penetration: the root has not fused through, caused by too small a gap, too little heat or fast travel. It is found by looking inside with a mirror or borescope, or by radiography, and prevented by the right gap and current and keeping a keyhole. Suck-back (concave root): the root sinks in, mostly at the bottom of a fixed pipe, caused by too much heat or too little filler. It is found inside by eye or by radiography, and prevented by adding enough rod and controlling heat overhead. Oxidised root (sugaring) on stainless: a grey, crusty root caused by poor or no back purge. It is found by eye inside, and prevented by purging to the right oxygen level. Tungsten inclusion: bits of tungsten in the root from dipping or overloading the tungsten. It shows as white spots on a radiograph, and is prevented by a steady hand and the right current and tungsten size.
markingPoints: Lack of penetration: cause, found by internal check or RT, prevention
Suck-back: cause, how found, prevention
Oxidised root or sugaring: poor purge, found by eye, prevented by purging
Tungsten inclusion: dipping or overloading, found by RT, prevention
Gives a cause, a method of finding and a prevention for each

essays.stem: Explain the hazards of argon purging and TIG welding in a confined space or a trench, and the controls you would put in place as team leader.
essays.modelAnswer: Argon has no smell or colour and is heavier than air, so it can collect in a trench, a pit or a tank and push out the oxygen. A person can collapse with no warning. Ozone and fume from the arc also build up in a small space, the heat is high, and getting someone out is hard. As team leader I would get a confined space permit and a hot work permit. The air would be tested for oxygen by a trained person before entry and watched during the work, with a personal oxygen alarm on the welder. The purge gas would be vented out of the space with a hose, and forced ventilation or extraction set up. Cylinders stay outside. A standby person stays at the opening with a way to talk to the welder and a rescue plan, and nobody goes in to rescue without the right equipment.
markingPoints: Argon is heavier than air, has no smell, and can push out oxygen
Ozone, fume, heat and difficult rescue
Permits; oxygen testing before and during work; personal oxygen alarm
Purge gas vented out; forced ventilation; cylinders outside
Standby person, communication and a rescue plan

essays.stem: Explain how a TIG procedure for a new job is trialled and approved, and what records (WPS, PQR and welder qualification) are kept.
essays.modelAnswer: First a draft WPS is written with the base metal, thickness, joint, filler, tungsten, gas and flow, purge, current and polarity, position, preheat and travel speed. A test piece is welded to the draft, with every setting recorded as it is used. The test piece is inspected by eye and then tested, for example by bend tests, macro-etch or radiography, as the standard for the job says. If it passes, the results and the real settings are written on a procedure qualification record (PQR), which supports the WPS. The WPS is then approved and issued to the welders. Each welder who will work on the job must pass a qualification test on that kind of joint and position, and their certificate is kept on file and checked to see it is still current. On the job, the welds are recorded against the WPS and the welder's ID.
markingPoints: Draft WPS with all the key settings
Test piece welded and settings recorded
Visual inspection and tests to the job's standard
PQR records the results and supports the approved WPS
Welder qualification tests, certificates kept current, welds recorded against WPS and welder

essays.stem: As team leader, describe how you would inspect and accept a batch of TIG-welded stainless steel handrail joints for a hotel in Montego Bay, and what you would put in the inspection report.
essays.modelAnswer: Before inspecting, I check the drawing and specification for the weld size, finish and any polish grade, and check my gauges and inspection light. I inspect every joint by eye: full fusion, even size, no cracks, pits, undercut or burn-through, and no dark heat tint left after cleaning. Handrail joints the public touch must be smooth and blended. Where the specification asks, I would test a sample with dye penetrant. Joints that do not meet the standard are tagged and kept apart, and a decision is made on repair. The report gives the job number, drawing and revision, the number of joints checked, the methods used, the results for each joint or batch, any faults with their location and what was done, the welders' IDs, and the date and my signature. Photos of typical welds and any faults are attached.
markingPoints: Checks the drawing and specification first; checks gauges and lighting
Visual check of every joint for fusion, profile, defects and heat tint
Dye penetrant on a sample where specified
Tags and separates rejects and decides on repairs
Report: job, drawing, numbers, methods, results, faults, welders, date, signature, photos

practical1.title: Planned TIG root and cap on a carbon steel pipe butt joint in the 5G position, with a weld record and inspection
practical1.brief: As a group, read the welding procedure the assessor gives you and plan the job together: the bevel and gap, the tungsten type and size, the filler rod, the current range and the gas flow. Each member then prepares and tacks one small-bore carbon steel pipe butt joint (about 50 mm to 100 mm outside diameter, the size the Centre has), fixes it with the axis horizontal (5G), and TIG welds the root and cap, working from the bottom to the top on each side. While one member welds, another acts as inspector: they check the fit-up and record the settings on the weld record. When the welds are cool, the group inspects each joint inside (with a mirror and torch) and outside, records the results, and the assessor cuts one strip from each joint for a bend test or a nick-break test. Photograph each stage and add the photos and records to the group's practical.
materials: Small-bore carbon steel pipe pieces with bevelled ends (two per member)
DC TIG machines with foot pedals or torch controls, and argon with flowmeters
Lanthanated or ceriated tungstens, and a grinder kept for tungsten
ER70S-2 or ER70S-6 filler rod, as the procedure gives
Pipe stands to fix the pipe in 5G
Inspection mirror, torch, weld gauge, and the procedure and weld record sheets
photos: A tungsten ground to a point, beside the tungsten grinder
A pipe pair tacked with an even gap
A member welding the root at the bottom of the pipe, in full PPE
The inside of each root, seen with a mirror
The bent or broken test strips, labelled by member
The completed weld record and the cleaned area
checklist: Took part in the plan and chose the right tungsten, filler and settings
Prepared and tacked the pipe with an even gap and clean ends
Ground the tungsten correctly on the right grinder
Welded the root with even penetration all round, changing angles as the position changed
Kept the hot rod end in the gas and avoided touching the tungsten
Finished cap even, with no undercut, porosity or cracks
Recorded settings and inspection results accurately as inspector
Closed the gas and left the area safe and clean
safety: Use extraction at the tungsten grinder; wear eye protection when grinding
Wear full PPE: TIG makes strong ultraviolet light even with little smoke
Cylinders chained upright; close the valve when the job is finished
Switch off the output before changing the tungsten
Treat pipes as hot; use tongs and mark them HOT
Only the assessor cuts and bends test strips; stand clear

practical2.title: TIG welding of stainless steel sheet with a back purge, followed by inspection and heat-tint cleaning
practical2.brief: As a group, plan and set up a back-purge for stainless steel sheet joints, using a purge channel or backing box with argon, and record the purge flow and time. Each member welds one butt joint in 1.5 mm to 2 mm grade 304 stainless sheet in the flat position with ER308L filler, and one outside corner joint, using low heat and tacking closely. A second member records the settings and the purge for each joint. When the welds are cool, the group inspects the front and back of every joint, compares the colours against a heat-tint chart, records the results, and cleans the heat tint by the method the Centre allows. Members then measure any distortion with a straight edge and record it. Photograph each stage and add the photos and records to the group's practical.
materials: Grade 304 stainless steel sheet, 1.5–2 mm, cut into pairs about 150 mm × 75 mm (two joints per member)
DC TIG machines with pedal or pulse, and argon for the torch and the purge
A purge channel, backing box or taped backing for the sheet, with a second flowmeter
Stainless-only brushes, clean solvent and lint-free cloths
Heat-tint chart, straight edge, feeler gauges and the record sheets
photos: The purge set-up with the second flowmeter
A joint cleaned and tacked closely
A member welding in full PPE
The front of each finished joint
The back of each joint against the heat-tint chart
A straight edge on a joint, showing any distortion
The completed records and the cleaned area
checklist: Helped set up the purge and recorded flow and time
Used only stainless-only brushes and tools on the sheet
Cleaned and tacked the joint closely
Kept heat low and travel steady, with filler added at the front of the pool
Front and back of the weld fully fused, with light colours and no sugaring
Recorded settings, colours and distortion accurately
Cleaned the heat tint safely by the approved method
safety: Keep solvents closed and away from the arc; let surfaces dry before welding
Vent purge gas safely; work in a well-ventilated area
Wear full PPE for the strong ultraviolet light
If any cleaning product is used, follow its label and SDS, and wear the gloves and eye protection it says
Cylinders chained upright; close valves after use
